source: Guo et al. (2026) SWE-Doctor, preliminary study: fail-to-fail reproduction tests
finding: Gap 8. Bug reproduction tests (BRTs) made by three strong generators were used as direct pass/fail targets for mini-SWE-agent. Tests that fail on the original code but also fail on the true fixed code (fail-to-fail, FF) hurt. Tests that fail then pass (FP) helped only a little and cover just one facet of the issue.
numbers: N=100 issues sampled from SWE-bench Verified. On FF issues the three BRT generators resolved 2, 3 and 3 fewer issues than plain mini-SWE-agent. The FP/FF count table is partly garbled in the text extract, so only the -2/-3/-3 line is certain.
quote: fail-to-fail BRTs, i.e., tests that fail on both the original and patched repositories, can mislead the agent
limits: Small sample (100). The generators are LLM test writers, not slice tools. Whether a test is FF is only known after the true patch exists, so the agent cannot sort FP from FF at run time.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a self-made failing test as ground truth. Use it as a source of runtime evidence (stack, values, executed lines), not as a target to make pass. An FF test pulls the agent away from the real fix.

source: Guo et al. (2026) SWE-Doctor, main results and ablation
finding: Gaps 1, 8. Turning a failing run into a structured runtime diagnosis (debugger expressions with values, executed branch, suspect code) beats using the test as a target. The diagnosis agent drives pdb itself. It is model-driven, not a code-computed slice.
numbers: SWE-bench Pro: +8.0 to +8.9 points over mini-SWE-agent and live-SWE-agent, 5 backends. Cost per issue $0.43 vs $0.23 and $0.22 (Verified); $0.64 vs $0.52 and $0.40 (Pro). So gains are NOT at equal cost. Ablation (50 Pro issues, GPT-5.4-mini): full 56.0%; removing the diagnosis stage costs 8.0 points; swapping multi-facet tests for other generators costs 8-10 points. On FF issues: 40.6% (plain) vs 53.1% (SWE-Doctor), column order inferred from the text. Five runs: mean 54.0%, SD 2.0; Pass@5 70.0%, All@5 40.0%. Go subset: 36.0% vs 32.0% and 30.0%.
limits: Ablations on 50 issues with one backend. More tokens than the baselines, so it does not answer the equal-token question. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Runtime evidence beats pass/fail targets, but at about 1.2 to 1.9 times the cost. Any claim for O5 must be reported at equal cost.

source: Haroon et al. (2026) Assessing the Impact of Code Changes on the Fault Localizability of LLMs, ICST 2026
finding: Gap 9. The 78% figure is real but it comes from LLMs reading code with a spec and no tools. Simple meaning-preserving edits (comments, names, dead code, formatting) make a model miss a fault it had found before. Nobody in this study used a tool-computed slice.
numbers: 750,013 fault-localisation tasks; 1,307 seed programs (637 Python, 670 Java); 4 fault types, 6 mutation kinds; 10 LLMs. 78% of previously correct localisations fail after mutation. Accuracy by mutation type: misleading names 29.02%, misleading comments 25.63%, dead code 20.38%. Dead-code strength 1 to 8: Java 15.82% to 8.57%, Python 42.88% to 29.34%. Faults in first quarter of file found most often. Open models drop most; Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini more robust.
quote: SPMs cause an LLM to fail to localize the same fault it correctly localized earlier in 78% of cases
limits: Single-file programs with specs, injected single-line faults, no repository, no tools, no agent loop. The paper itself names slicing as future work. Accuracies are low even before mutation, so 78% is a conditional flip rate.
agent_relevance: A slice computed by program analysis ignores comments, names and unreachable code by construction (my inference, not tested here). That is a reason to compute the slice by tool, but the test has not been run.

source: Wu et al. (2026) CausalRepair, ISSTA 2026: ablation of slice context
finding: Gaps 1, 6. A tool-computed dynamic slice of the failing run (plus a trimmed slice of the test) is the main source of gain in an LLM repair loop. All LLM methods were rerun on one backbone (DeepSeek-V3) and the slice is built from the execution trace by code.
numbers: Defects4J (483 single-function bugs): CausalRepair 313 correct; ReinFix 236; TSAPR 224; plain DeepSeek-V3 157. Ablation drops: no source dynamic slice -26.5% (230 fixes); test side with failing line only -38.3% (193); test side with the full test -10.0% (282); no iterative repair -18.5% (255); no patch augmentation -16.9% (260). Cost: $0.029 and 23.28 min per bug (2.53 min is slicing); money cost 17.9% of ReinFix. Gains saturate at 5 attempts and 3 turns.
limits: Java only; Defects4J is likely in training data. The source-slice ablation compares slice vs no slice, not slice vs free exploration. Attempts were set to the chosen optimum, not matched to baselines.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that a code-computed causal slice helps a model, at lower cost. Noise matters as much as absence: the full test hurt by 10%, the bare failing line by 38%. So the slice should be focused, not minimal.

source: Wu et al. (2026) CausalRepair on Defects4J-Trans (semantic-preserving rewrites)
finding: Gap 9. Defects4J-Trans applies meaning-preserving transformations to the 483 single-function bugs. A repair loop that feeds a tool-computed dynamic slice kept most of its score. A plain model lost far more.
numbers: Defects4J-Trans, 483 bugs: CausalRepair 289 (144 on V1.2, 145 on V2.0); ReinFix 200; plain DeepSeek-V3 97. Same methods on the original: 313; 236; 157. Relative drops: CausalRepair -7.7%, ReinFix -15%, plain model -38%.
limits: Different task (repair, tests available) from the 78% study (localisation, spec only). Drop figures are my arithmetic from two tables with the same 483-bug base. Includes test slicing and iterative repair, so the slice alone is not isolated. Trans release (Oct 2024) is after the DeepSeek-V3 cutoff, so contamination is also lowered.
agent_relevance: Weak but real support that a tool-built slice makes localisation less sensitive to surface edits. Run the mutation test on our own slice step before trusting it.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2026) Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures, results at equal budget
finding: Gap 6. Comparison at an equal number of calls (six plain fresh samples vs six trace-guided repair attempts). A line-by-line trace added to assertion failures beats fresh sampling on BigCodeBench, ties on HumanEval, loses on LiveCodeBench. Traces work when the failing input is visible and the bug is an implementation slip.
numbers: Qwen2.5 Instruct 7B/14B/32B/72B, one run each. BigCodeBench (1,140 tasks): one trace repairs 299 of the repair set (29.5%) vs 227 (22.4%) for fresh sampling; the conclusion text says 26.7%, so the paper is inconsistent on this figure. Pooled accuracy 71.9% to 78.4%. HumanEval: 40 failures, trace 21 vs 20 fresh, a tie. LiveCodeBench (175): trace 4.9% vs fresh 6.5%. Assertion failures are 79.0% (BCB), 100% (HE), 93.2% (LCB) of residual failures. Identical resubmissions fall 28% to 8% (BCB). Showing all traces was worse than showing one on every benchmark.
limits: Single run, no variance. Small Qwen models only. Traces are whole-function line traces, not slices. Repair, not localisation.
agent_relevance: Disagreement in K10 is mostly about the task, not the idea: traces help implementation slips with visible inputs, not misread problems or algorithm errors. One focused trace beats many.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2026) token cost of traces and break-even rule
finding: Gaps 1, 6. A trace makes every call longer but can cut the number of calls. It pays off only when calls fall by more than 1 - 1/k, where k is the length increase per call.
numbers: One trace: k=1.15 to 1.21, break-even 13-17% fewer calls. Calls fell 16% (BCB) and 30% (HE), so total tokens -3.9% (BCB) and -16.0% (HE); on LCB calls fell only 3% and tokens rose 16.7%. All traces: k=1.50 to 1.70, tokens +28.2% (BCB), +19.1% (HE), +48.9% (LCB); never pays for itself.
limits: Qwen tokeniser, single run, pooled over four model sizes.
agent_relevance: Gives a simple budget rule for our agent: an evidence step should shorten the loop by more than it lengthens each call, else resample.

source: Lee et al. (2025) debug-gym, SWE-bench-Lite table
finding: Gaps 1, 6. Giving an agent pdb (the model chooses where to look) helps strong models and hurts some weak ones. Giving pdb only after 5 failed rewrites (debug(5)) was best or near best for every model.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite, 300 tasks, 3 runs, success %: rewrite / debug / debug(5): GPT-4o 19.1 / 17.2 / 23.6; 4o-mini 4.0 / 3.5 / 6.2; o1-preview 10.7 / 30.2 / 30.8; o3-mini 8.5 / 22.1 / 19.8; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 37.2 / 48.4 / 52.1; Llama-3.3-70B 2.4 / 4.0 / 4.8. On Aider (simple tasks) pdb gave no clear effect.
limits: Column order read from a garbled table extract but consistent with the text (weak models hurt by early pdb). Debugger use is model-driven, so this is free exploration with a tool, not a slice. Episode length and tokens rose with pdb.
agent_relevance: Fits the idea of switching late: use the costly evidence step after cheap attempts stall, not from step one. Gain depends on the model.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: how its confidence is made and what it costs
finding: Gap 7. The AutoFL confidence is agreement across 5 separate runs (self-consistency), not a token probability. So it cannot gate extra steps for free: it needs the runs first.
numbers: Spearman between confidence and Precision@1: +0.57 (Defects4J), +0.52 (BugsInPy), p<0.0001; with reciprocal rank +0.67 / +0.50; with average precision +0.70 / +0.49. Five runs per bug (diminishing returns beyond 5), gpt-3.5-turbo-0613. Explanations: 20% of 300 sampled accurate; 26.3% contain an inaccurate statement.
limits: GPT-3.5 era. Correlation is rank-based, not a calibrated threshold. No token accounting for the 5 runs.
agent_relevance: Confidence from agreement costs about 5x tokens. A cheaper gate (for example: does the cited line appear in the code-computed slice?) is untested.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: tool-call budget
finding: Gaps 4, 7. A free-exploration agent with function-retrieval tools used few steps, and raising the step cap hurt.
numbers: Average 5.37 function calls per run. Cap of 10 chosen because fewer than 10% of runs reached it. A cap of 20 made the model overflow context and cut performance by about half.
limits: GPT-3.5 with a small context window; a modern long-context model may not collapse the same way.
agent_relevance: Free exploration has a hard length ceiling in context. This supports handing long dependence chains to a tool rather than letting steps pile up.

source: Kang et al. (2023) AutoSD: LLM-driven scientific debugging (hypothesis, prediction, experiment, observation, conclusion)
finding: Gap 3. A structured hypothesis log with real debugger experiments did not beat asking the model to fix directly, but it gave explanations and a usable done-signal. Real execution results mattered: replacing them with model-imagined output lowered reliability.
numbers: Defects4J correct fixes (AutoSD vs plain LLM): v1.2 76 vs 87; v2.0 113 vs 110. With real execution, runs predicting DONE were 12.4 points more likely plausible; with the debugger imagined by the model, 11 points less likely. Plausible patch in 73% of runs with real debugger vs 63% without. DONE-flagged plausible patches 89% correct vs 82% for others. Human study N=20 (8 undergraduates, 6 graduates, 6 professionals): more accurate with explanations on 7 of 12 patches, time about the same; 70% said explanations matter.
limits: ChatGPT-era model. Compares a hypothesis log to direct repair, not a hypothesis log to a plain hypothesis list or to why-questions. Human study is patch review, not debugging.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis list alone is not shown to raise repair. What helps is checking each hypothesis against executed evidence. Matches K11: do not trust imagined execution.

source: Kong et al. (2024) ContrastRepair: contrastive passing/failing test pairs
finding: Gap 3. Showing the model a failing test next to the most similar passing test (a contrast, close in spirit to asking why this input fails and that one does not) improves repair over failing-test-only feedback. Random pairs help less.
numbers: 106 bugs, mean of 3 runs: full 37.00 correct and 60.33 plausible; no pair 30.67 and 48.00; random pair 34.00 and 56.33. Overall 360 of 581 bugs fixed vs 334 for ChatRepair; 20.91% fewer API calls than ChatRepair.
limits: ChatGPT-3.5-era, Java. Pair selection by similarity is the authors' design. This is contrast evidence, not a why-not question as users ask it.
agent_relevance: Best available LLM analogue of a why-not step: contrast the failing case against a near passing case. Cheap to try as a step before localising.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug: explanation and trace feedback
finding: Gap 3. Asking the model to explain its code line by line (rubber duck) helps a little; adding unit-test results and execution trace helps more. The model writes the trace itself.
numbers: Spider text-to-SQL (no unit tests): explanation gives +2 to 3%, +9% on hardest queries. TransCoder and MBPP with tests: up to +12%; explanation alone +2 to 3% on translation. StarCoder: +6% on MBPP with trace. Matches baselines that sample over 10 times more programs.
limits: Model-written traces can be wrong. Few-shot prompts. Older models (code-davinci-002, GPT-3.5, GPT-4).
agent_relevance: A plain explain-then-check step is a small gain; real test results carry most of the benefit. No why-did vs why-not split was tested.

source: Chen et al. (2025) LocAgent: graph-guided code localisation on SWE-bench Lite
finding: Gap 1. A tool-built dependency graph (imports, calls, inheritance) with a multi-hop traversal tool beat free-exploration agents using the same Claude-3.5 model. It is a dependency graph, not a backward slice from the failure.
numbers: SWE-bench-Lite, 274 examples. File-level Acc@5 with Claude-3.5: LocAgent 94.16; SWE-agent and OpenHands 90.15; Agentless 79.56; BM25 61.68. Function-level Acc@10 about 86.5 vs 83.2 (OpenHands). Cost per example: Qwen2.5-7B fine-tuned $0.05; LocAgent with Claude cheaper than OpenHands per Table 5. Performance falls for all methods as graph distance between issue text and patched function grows (hop 0 to 3+); agents degrade less than non-agents.
limits: Cost is comparable but tokens were not matched. Localisation only (file and function level, not line). Garbled table extract: rank order is certain, small gaps are not.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is partly answered: a code-computed graph helps by about 4 points at file level at similar or lower cost. No study found that computes a failure-backward slice for an SWE-bench agent.

source: Li, Su, Lyu (2026) RepoReason: re-check of thresholds and what they measure
finding: Gap 4. The 20-source / 600-line / 100-step numbers describe where models fail at predicting a program value from code, using the slice only as a ruler. They were not tested as switch points for a tool.
numbers: 2,492 tasks (Easy 1009, Medium 838, Hard 645), 7 Python repositories, 5 models. Mean slice volume 393.6 lines (SD 706.3); mean chain length 93.9 (SD 198.0). Accuracy below 40% for most models when over 20 independent upstream sources, except Claude. Cliff after 600 lines; consistency loss beyond 100 steps. Temperature 0 vs 1 shifts overall accuracy by 1.0 point.
limits: Task is abductive assertion checking, not bug localisation. Mean chain length (94) is already near the 100-step mark, so the cliff is not a rare corner. Thresholds are read from plots.
agent_relevance: Use as a rough alarm, not a rule: if the computed slice is over about 600 lines or 100 steps, or has over 20 inputs, stop reasoning over it whole and split it. Needs testing on our agent.

source: Soremekun, Kirschner, Boehme, Zeller (2021) Locating Faults with Program Slicing: An Empirical Analysis (arXiv preprint of EMSE paper)
finding: Gaps 4, 5. A simulated programmer who follows dependencies in dynamic slices finds single faults sooner than one who follows a statistical ranking. Best is a hybrid: look at the top few ranked lines first, then switch to the slice.
numbers: 457 bugs (369 single, 88 multiple) in 46 C programs; 295 real single faults, 74 injected single, 88 injected multi. Dynamic slicing 8 points more effective than the best statistical formula on single faults; finds the fault earlier for 66% of bugs. Statistical debugging localises 33% of faults at the single top line. Hybrid (top 5 then slice): 98% of errors within top-20 statements vs about 100 lines for either alone; average 15% (30 lines) of code. Statistical debugging is better on multiple faults.
limits: Code-inspection simulation with no human or LLM participants. C programs, test suites given. This is the closest later check of slices as a search unit but does not test human cognition.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'cheap guess first, switch to computed slice when the guess fails' (switch after about 5 candidates). Single-fault bias: with several faults, slices lose.

source: Chang et al. (2025) SliceMate, downstream bug localisation (RQ2)
finding: Gap 1. Slices made by an LLM agent improve two existing bug-localisation tools more than slices from other slicers. This compares slicers, not slice vs no slice.
numbers: Defects4J and BugsInPy. Up to 34% better localisation than other slicing inputs; up to 12% more buggy-code coverage in slices. BugsInPy with IncBL: Top-1/3/5/10 = 0.19, 0.43, 0.57, 0.70. On 2,200 SliceBench cases: up to 63.1% higher Accuracy and 62.5% higher F1 than best baseline on large programs. Removing verification and refinement agents cuts F1 by 5.5% to 29.1%.
limits: Static slicing by LLM agents, not code-computed. Baselines are other slicers. Not an issue-resolution agent.
agent_relevance: Does not show slice beats no slice. Shows that slice quality matters and that an LLM-made slice can be checked and refined.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? ISSTA (author PDF)
finding: Gap 2 closed for the numbers. Students debugged two programs (Tetris, NanoXML) with or without a Tarantula-ranked statement list in Eclipse. The tool did not help overall. It helped only the high performers on the easy task. Moving the faulty line up or down the ranking changed nothing significant. Programmers jumped around the list instead of reading top to bottom, and kept inspecting after they had already seen the faulty line.
numbers: Main experiment 24 students (groups A and B), 30 min per task; an earlier 34-student run had a flawed NanoXML ranking; 10 extra students (C and D) for the rank manipulation. Mean successful times (min:sec) Tetris/NanoXML: A 8:51/22:30, B 14:28/20:16, C 10:12/15:12, D 12:36/18:30. Overall difference not significant by two-tailed t-test. High performers (N=10, completed both tasks): 8:51 vs 14:28 on Tetris, p<0.05. Completers: 18 on Tetris vs 10 on NanoXML. Ratio of Tetris to NanoXML time 2.5 vs 1.3 (p<0.02), so no extra benefit on the harder task. Rank manipulation: Tetris fault 7 to 35, NanoXML fault 83 to 16; no significant effect, same ratio .79 in both groups. Navigation (22 usable logs): 37% of visits jumped more than one position, mean skip 10, mean 10.3 zigzags (range 1-36). Of 10 who clicked the faulty line, only 1 stopped; others kept using the tool about 10 more minutes, 61% of time after first seeing the fault.
quote: programmers do not visit each statement in a linear fashion
limits: Graduate students at one school, two small programs, statistical-debugging ranked list (not a slice or why-question tool). The group labels in the text are confusing (tool and non-tool groups are swapped in places), so quote only the stated t-tests. The paper also reviews Whyline (20 subjects, twice as fast) without replicating it.
agent_relevance: A ranked list of suspicious lines is not understanding: finding the fault line did not end the search. For our agent, a slice or suspect list must come with the causal path (why this line), and the agent must still test whether the line explains the failure. Evidence against showing bare ranks.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011), section 2: summary of Weiser and later slicing studies
finding: Gap 5 partly closed, second-hand. A reviewer who opened the originals says Weiser's first study did not test whether slices help debugging. It tested whether programmers recognise slices after debugging. Slices were recognised significantly more often than other fragments. Later studies testing slicing tools found no benefit (Weiser and Lyle), a benefit only on a 25-line program with paper printouts, mixed benefit in small studies (Kusumoto), and only 4 of 17 students slicing instinctively (Francel and Rugaber).
numbers: Weiser: 21 programmers, 3 programs of 75-150 lines (earlier line a02 said two programs; this source says three). Weiser and Lyle: one 100-line program, no improvement; follow-up on 25 lines with printouts and dicing, faster on some bugs. Francel and Rugaber: 17 students, 4 sliced instinctively, those 4 understood a 200-line program better. Kusumoto: 6 students; 9 faults in 3 programs (about 400 lines) no significant difference; 6 faults in 6 programs of 25-52 lines, significant for some programs only. Sherwood and Murphy: 6 subjects, no definitive result. Weiser's own test statistics were not given and not verified.
quote: slices were recognized significantly more often than other fragments
limits: Second-hand summary. Weiser 1982 PDF still unopened; its p-values and exact N per test remain unverified. Recognition is not use.
agent_relevance: The 'slice as natural cognitive unit' claim is recognition evidence only. Tool-benefit evidence from slicing tools is mixed and weaker than the Whyline story. Keep K14 as motivation, and K02 should name these null results.

source: Semantic Scholar citation list for Parnin and Orso (2011): 2026 papers to read next
finding: Leads only. Citing papers include 'Do Coding Agents Still Need a Debugger? Frontier-Model-Based Fault Localization at the Accuracy Ceiling' (2026, no open PDF found), 'CoReX: Context-Aware Refinement-Based Slicing for Debugging Regression Failures' (2026), 'Data-Oriented Debugging Across Place and Time' (2026) and 'A Grounded Theory of Debugging in Professional Software Engineering Practice' (2026). Only titles were seen. arXiv and OpenAlex searches were rate-limited, so none were opened.
numbers: Parnin and Orso: 666 citations as reported by the API.
limits: Titles only. The first title (frontier-model fault localisation vs debugger) could not be opened; web search returned only a secondary summary claiming 96.7-99.9% static localisation accuracy on short single-fault programs. Not used as evidence.
agent_relevance: Open these first in the next pass; the first could test debugger tools on frontier-model agents.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Coherence Collapse: Diagnosing Why Code Agents Fail After Reaching the Right Code (TrajEval)
finding: Gap 1, indirect. On SWE-bench Verified, capable code agents mostly find the right place and still fail. So a better localiser (such as a computed slice) has limited headroom for strong models. Weak models do fail at search.
numbers: 16,758 trajectories, 3 agent scaffolds, 7 models, SWE-bench Verified and PolyBench Verified. 60-69% of failures of capable models on SWE-Agent and OpenHands reached and edited the correct functions yet gave wrong patches. Edit-Quality bucket 56.9% of SWE-Agent failures on SWE-bench. Qwen3-8B failures concentrate at Search (41.1%); Search share rises from 19.3% (SWE-bench) to 47.0% (PolyBench). Of 914 edit-quality failures, 39.7% coherence collapse (agent reaches and then overwrites correct code). Consensus-driven confirmatory feedback on GPT-5: 69.0% vs 66.0%, McNemar p=0.08, n=500.
quote: The dominant failure of capable models is not localization
limits: Reference-patch alignment is a proxy; no slice tool was tested; one (model, scaffold) cell for the intervention; not at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 is not answered by any head-to-head: no study found compares a code-computed slice with free exploration at equal tokens on SWE-bench. Where the agent is strong, effort should go to keeping a verified fix and checking it, not only to localisation. Slice help matters most for weaker models and multi-language repos.

source: Sepidband et al. (2026) RGFL: Reasoning Guided Fault Localization (explanations per candidate)
finding: Gap 3, partly. Asking the model to write a bug-specific explanation for each candidate file and element (why this could be the cause, and its limitation) then re-ranking improved localisation and repair over Agentless. The explanation text itself carries the gain: embedding the explanations instead of letting the LLM rank them did not help.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified file-level Hit@1 71.4% to 85%, MRR 81.8% to 88.8%. Element-level exact match (top-3 files) 36% to 69%. End-to-end repair success +12.8% when integrated into Agentless. Embedding re-rankers: Hit@1 64.4% (Gemini-embedding-001), 60.8% (Voyage 3.5), 52% (text-embedding-3-small), at or below baseline. OrcaLoca slightly better at Hit@1 on Verified and Lite.
quote: natural language reasoning itself--not just its embedding representation--is essential
limits: Pipeline (Agentless), not an agent loop. No why-not versus why-did comparison and no hypothesis-list control; explanations are for candidates, not for the failing output. Cost at equal tokens not checked.
agent_relevance: A per-candidate 'why would this cause the failure, and what does it fail to explain' step is a cheap O5-style check with measured gains. It does not settle whether the why-not form beats a hypothesis list; that stays untested.

source: Garg and Huang (2026) Debug2Fix: Can Interactive Debugging Help Coding Agents Fix More Bugs?
finding: Gaps 3 and 6. The main agent asks a debug subagent natural-language runtime questions ('what exception occurs when running X', 'what is the value of V at L'). Raw debugger tools handed to the main agent did not help; the question-and-answer wrapper did, but only when the prompt forced its use.
numbers: GitBug-Java: GPT-5 60.2% to 73.1% (over 20% relative), Sonnet 4.5 about +13%, Haiku 4.5 about +16%; call rate over 98% with the tool-limit strategy, much lower without. SWE-Bench-Live: GPT-5 call rate over 60% and +16%. Direct debug tools without the subagent: flat or worse (for example 64.5 (-14.8%) in one cell, 33.3 (-6.7%) in another). Subagent capped at 25 steps. Token cost rose in all configs (for example 802k, +131%, in one setup).
quote: better tool design is often just as important as switching to a more expensive model
limits: Preprint, three models, same model for main and sub agent, call rate differs by model and language. Questions are about runtime values, not why-not events; question types were not ablated. Table cells were read from a garbled extract.
agent_relevance: Supports asking a bounded question about runtime state and getting a short evidence-backed answer, rather than dumping raw traces on the agent. Helps explain the trace contradiction (gap 6): focused answers help, whole-trace dumps often do not. Cost rises.

source: Bansal et al. (2026) VibePass: self-generated fault-triggering tests and fault hypotheses
finding: Gaps 8 and 3. With 12 frontier models, the bottleneck is forming the hypothesis about which input exposes the bug, not writing a valid test. A self-made test that really exposes the fault repairs as well as an external one. A test that fails to expose the fault makes repair worse than no test, and on average both internal and external tests did not beat the no-test baseline.
numbers: 173 instances, 12 frontier LLMs, competitive-programming problems with LLM-written buggy solutions. Settings NoTest, ExtTest, IntTest. Exact per-model Pass@1 not extracted here.
quote: fault hypothesis generation--not output validation--as the dominant bottleneck
limits: Short single-file programs; no slicing or why-not prompts tested; numbers read only from abstract and discussion text.
agent_relevance: Agrees with SWE-Doctor (d01): a reproduction that does not witness the real fault is worse than none. Add a gate: check that the reproduction fails for the reported reason before using it. Hypothesis quality is the weak step, where a why-question could help but is untested here.
